extracted.intended_audience: inventors, entrepreneurs, startup founders, in-house counsel, and businesses deciding between trade secret and patent protection (U.S.-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical decision guide for whether to protect an invention as a trade secret or by filing a patent (with hybrid and procedural considerations), focused on U.S. law and commercial strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic value from secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a trade secret under U.S. law, the information must derive value from not being generally known to competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the competitive advantage disappears once information is public, it likely lacks the necessary economic value for trade secret protection. Examples given: Coca‑Cola formula, KFC spices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not readily ascertainable
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade secret must not be easily obtained by others through legitimate means; it should not be readily ascertainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether competitors could discover the information by reverse engineering, public sources, or routine analysis. Proprietary server‑side algorithms and internal manufacturing steps are typical examples that may be not readily ascertainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners must take reasonable steps to keep the information confidential (e.g., NDAs, access controls, employee training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider whether confidentiality procedures were implemented; merely labeling information a 'trade secret' is insufficient. Examples of reasonable measures: NDAs, compartmentalization (split suppliers), vaults, security policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligible subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a patent, the invention must be a patent‑eligible type: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (not abstract ideas or laws of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the invention falls within statutory subject matter before evaluating novelty/non‑obviousness. U.S. case law and PTO guidance affect borderline areas (e.g., software/business methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel (35 U.S.C. § 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention must be novel — not previously known or used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior public disclosures, sales, or patents can defeat novelty. Use prior art searches and document invention dates carefully; public disclosure may trigger the U.S. 1‑year bar and devastate foreign rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obvious (35 U.S.C. § 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable invention must involve an inventive step — it must not be an obvious improvement to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent prosecution and claim drafting should focus on demonstrating technical differences and unexpected benefits. Obviousness analysis is fact‑intensive and often disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately described (enablement / written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must teach others how to make and use the invention; the disclosure must be sufficiently detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft applications with enabling examples, embodiments, and sufficient detail to support the full scope of claimed subject matter. Lack of adequate description can lead to rejection or invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration (trade secret vs patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets: indefinite duration so long as secrecy is maintained; Utility patents: 20 years from filing (design patents: 15 years from grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the competitive advantage is expected to last well beyond 20 years, trade secret protection may be preferable. Patents provide a fixed monopoly term but then public domain access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets do not require public disclosure; patents require a public disclosure (application is published ~18 months after filing unless withheld).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure of how the invention works would destroy its value even after patent expiration, prefer trade secret. Filing a provisional application still involves an eventual path to public disclosure if converted to a non‑provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost (relative expense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secret protection is relatively low cost (NDAs, policies, security); patenting is comparatively expensive ($5,000–$20,000+ over the patent lifetime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cash constraints of startups; provisional applications (~$2,000) can be an interim measure. Include prosecution, maintenance, and enforcement costs in budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection scope (misappropriation vs exclusivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets protect against misappropriation (theft, breach of confidence); patents grant exclusivity that prevents others from making, using, selling, or importing the invention even if independently developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If independent invention or reverse engineering is a realistic threat, patents provide broader legal protection. Trade secrets only provide remedies when confidentiality is breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration required
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets: no registration required; Patent: must file an application and obtain a USPTO grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic protection for trade secrets is contingent on secrecy measures. Patent protection requires meeting statutory criteria and navigating prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent invention risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If a competitor independently invents the same thing, trade secret law provides no protection, whereas a patent lets you stop independent inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the market or field has many actors likely to independently develop similar solutions, patents are often necessary to secure exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse-engineering risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If competitors can buy and analyze your product to discover how it works, trade secrets are ineffective; patents can prevent copying even after reverse engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess visibility of internal processes/components. Examples: consumer electronics, chemical compounds, and distributed software are often reverse‑engineerable and thus better candidates for patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secret enforcement requires proving misappropriation (can be difficult); patent enforcement requires proving infringement (claim comparison against accused product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidentiary burdens and litigation complexity. Trade secret cases hinge on showing improper acquisition/use; patent cases hinge on claim construction and technical comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of loss (fragility vs permanence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets carry high risk of permanent loss if disclosed; patents, once granted, are robust for the term unless invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh operational risks (employee leaks, supplier exposures) against patent prosecution and validity risks. If disclosure would be catastrophic, consider trade secret only if secrecy controls are reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for trade secret: invention cannot be reverse-engineered
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets are preferable when the invention is a process, formula, or algorithm that is not visible in the final product and cannot be readily deduced by analyzing the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Coca‑Cola formula, internal synthesis routes, server‑side algorithms. Security measures like compartmentalization can enhance viability (e.g., splitting recipe parts among suppliers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for trade secret: need for protection beyond 20 years
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose trade secret if you can maintain confidentiality for decades and the competitive advantage is expected to outlast a patent term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic example: Coca‑Cola maintaining secrecy for 130+ years. If long‑lived commercial advantage is expected, trade secrets may outperform a 20‑year patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for trade secret: want to avoid public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosing how the invention works (even temporarily) would eliminate competitive advantage, trade secret protection is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If public disclosure would enable competitors to substitute or improve products even after patent expiry, avoid patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for trade secret: patent costs are prohibitive
rubrics_metrics.description: If the organization cannot afford patent prosecution and maintenance costs, trade secret protection (with NDAs and security) may be the only viable option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider provisional filings as a lower‑cost intermediate step; weigh investor expectations (VCs often prefer patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for trade secret: technology is rapidly evolving
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention will be obsolete before a patent issues or before the patent term would yield value, trade secret or other strategies may be preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents take 2–4 years to grant; for short product lifecycles, the delay and cost may not be worth it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for patent: invention can be reverse-engineered
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are preferable when competitors can analyze your product and replicate it, because patents prevent copying even after reverse engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mechanical devices, chemical compounds, distributed software—use patents to secure exclusivity against reverse engineers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for patent: need to publicly commercialize
rubrics_metrics.description: When selling the product will inherently reveal how it works (making secrecy impossible), patent protection is usually necessary to protect value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the product's nature exposes the invention, rely on patents to retain exclusivity while selling broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for patent: need to raise funding or attract acquirers
rubrics_metrics.description: Investors and acquirers often value patents more than trade secrets because patents provide clear, enforceable exclusivity and are easier to value and transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many VCs expect patent‑pending status; choose patents (or provisional filings) when investor signaling and M&A readiness are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for patent: want to stop independent invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If preventing others who independently invent the same technology is important, patents are the tool to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents eliminate independent invention as a defense — critical in crowded or fast‑moving technical fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for patent: want to license the technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are easier to license because claims define the scope; trade secret licensing requires disclosure to licensees and introduces additional risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If monetization via licensing is part of the business model, patents typically facilitate transactions and valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid strategy: patent core innovation, keep implementation details as trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent the fundamental invention while keeping specific manufacturing processes, optimization techniques, or quality control methods confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: pharmaceutical companies patent the compound but keep synthesis routes and formulations secret. This maximizes protection breadth while preserving operational advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid strategy: patent visible features, keep back-end processes secret
rubrics_metrics.description: For software and similar systems, patent user‑facing or observable features and keep server‑side algorithms, data processing, and optimization techniques as trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach protects what competitors can observe while preserving indefinite secrecy over internal methods, subject to adequate security measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid strategy: use provisional patent application to preserve options
rubrics_metrics.description: File a provisional application to establish a filing date, then use the 12 months to test the market, seek funding, and decide whether to proceed with a full utility application or keep the invention as a trade secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional costs cited (~$2,000); filing preserves a date but eventual non‑provisional pursuit will lead to public disclosure if prosecuted. Use provisional strategically if you want to delay full prosecution or retain options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: assuming you can 'try trade secret first, patent later'
rubrics_metrics.description: Public disclosure or offering the invention for sale can forfeit patent rights (subject to a 1‑year U.S. grace period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publicly reveal or commercially exploit an invention if you plan to file patents later — international rights are especially vulnerable because most foreign jurisdictions lack a grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: failing to implement reasonable security measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling something a trade secret without NDAs, access controls, and training can cause courts to rule you forfeited protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document confidentiality programs, maintain NDAs with employees and vendors, and use technical and organizational safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: choosing trade secrets for easily reverse-engineered products
rubrics_metrics.description: If the product can be disassembled and analyzed, trade secret protection is illusory and you should pursue patents instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the physical and analytical accessibility of your product before deciding; consumer electronics and sold chemicals are poor trade secret candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: choosing patents for internal processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing patents on internal manufacturing processes that cannot be seen by competitors forces public disclosure with little practical benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If competitors cannot observe and need to duplicate the process, prefer trade secret protection to avoid unnecessary disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistake: ignoring the 1‑year grace period deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S. you generally have a 1‑year grace period to file after public disclosure or sale; missing this can forfeit patent rights and many foreign rights have no grace period at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track disclosures and filing deadlines closely; when in doubt, file a provisional or non‑provisional application before public disclosure.
